questions.q: `x = jnp.zeros(3); x[0] = 1` raises an error. What is the JAX way to set an element?
options: `x = x.at[0].set(1)`, which returns a new array
questions.why: JAX arrays are immutable. `.at[...]` expresses the update functionally, and under `jit` XLA usually performs it in place anyway.

questions.q: What does `x.at[jnp.array([1, 1])].add(5)` do to `x = jnp.zeros(3)`?
options: Raises an error for repeated indices
questions.why: `.at[].add` is a scatter-add, so both updates land on index 1, like `np.add.at`.

questions.q: Why does JAX require explicit PRNG keys instead of a global seed?
options: Functions stay pure, so results don't depend on hidden state, which matters for jit, vmap and parallelism
questions.why: Hidden global state would make traced and vectorised functions non-reproducible. Every random call takes a key explicitly.

questions.q: You call `jax.random.normal(key, ...)` twice with the same `key`. What happens?
options: You get identical numbers both times; split the key first
questions.why: The same key always produces the same output. `key, sub = jax.random.split(key)` gives a fresh subkey for each use.

questions.q: Inside `jax.jit`, why does `x[x > 0]` fail?
options: Boolean arrays aren't allowed in JAX
Its output shape depends on the data, and jit needs static shapes
questions.why: Under tracing the number of selected elements is unknown. Use `jnp.where(mask, x, 0)` with masked sums and counts instead.

questions.q: To compute the mean of the positive entries under jit, which is correct?
questions.why: Masked reductions keep shapes fixed. The `maximum(..., 1)` guards the all-negative case.

questions.q: Why pad variable-length batches up to a few fixed "bucket" lengths in JAX?
options: Each new shape triggers a recompilation, so bucketing bounds the number of compiled versions
questions.why: jit caches one compiled program per input shape. Padding to, say, 128, 256 and 512 means at most three compilations.

questions.q: What is the default float dtype of `jnp.array(1.0)`?
questions.why: JAX defaults to 32-bit for accelerator performance. `jax.config.update('jax_enable_x64', True)` enables float64.

questions.q: `jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn, has_aux=True)` expects `loss_fn` to return what?
options: A tuple `(loss, aux)`, and it returns `((loss, aux), grads)`
questions.why: `has_aux` lets you return metrics such as accuracy alongside the scalar being differentiated, without differentiating them.

questions.q: `jax.grad(f)` requires `f` to return what?
questions.why: `grad` is for scalar outputs. For vector outputs use `jax.jacfwd`, `jax.jacrev`, `jax.vjp` or `jax.jvp`.

questions.q: A Hessian-vector product computed as `jax.jvp(jax.grad(f), (x,), (v,))[1]` costs about...
options: A small constant times one gradient evaluation, without forming the Hessian
questions.why: Forward-over-reverse differentiates the gradient in direction $v$. It is the standard way to get curvature information for large models.

questions.q: Per-example gradients for a batch are computed with...
questions.why: `vmap` maps over the batch axis of the data while sharing `params` (`None`), giving one gradient per example, which DP-SGD needs for per-example clipping.

questions.q: A straight-through estimator for rounding uses `custom_vjp`. What does the backward rule return?
options: Zero, the true derivative of rounding
The upstream gradient unchanged, as if rounding were the identity
The gradient times the quantisation step
questions.why: Rounding has zero derivative almost everywhere, which would stop learning. Pretending it is the identity in the backward pass lets fake-quantised training work.

questions.q: A simpler way to write a straight-through estimator without `custom_vjp` is...
questions.why: The forward value is `round(x)`, but the gradient only sees the `x` term because the difference is wrapped in `stop_gradient`.

questions.q: `jax.jacfwd` versus `jax.jacrev`: which is cheaper for a function from $\mathbb R^{1000}$ to $\mathbb R^{3}$?
options: `jacrev`, which needs one pass per output (3)
`jacfwd`, which needs one pass per input (1000)
questions.why: Reverse mode scales with the number of outputs, forward mode with the number of inputs. Wide-to-narrow functions favour reverse mode.

questions.q: What does `jax.lax.stop_gradient(x)` do in the forward pass?
options: Nothing; it returns `x` unchanged and only blocks gradients
Detaches and copies `x` to host memory
questions.why: It is the identity in value and zero in derivative, used for targets, straight-through tricks and target networks.

questions.q: A function's window size changes the output shape. How do you jit it?
options: Pass it as a traced array
Mark the window as static with `static_argnums` or `static_argnames`
questions.why: Static arguments are part of the cache key and are known as Python values during tracing, so shapes can depend on them. Each distinct value triggers a compile.

questions.q: Inside a jitted function, `if x > 0:` on a traced array raises an error. What should you use?
questions.why: Python control flow needs concrete values, which tracers don't have. `lax.cond` compiles both branches and picks one at run time.

questions.q: A learning-rate schedule receives the step count as a traced array. Which is valid inside jit?
questions.why: JAX operations accept tracers; Python's `math` functions and `int()` need concrete numbers.

questions.q: Why use `jax.lax.scan` instead of a Python `for` loop under jit?
options: The Python loop is unrolled into the compiled graph, so long loops compile slowly; `scan` compiles the body once
questions.why: Unrolling 1,000 steps makes a program 1,000 times larger. `scan` keeps compile time constant and still supports autodiff.

questions.q: `lax.scan(f, init, xs)` expects `f` to return what?
options: `(new_carry, y)`, where the `y`s are stacked into the second output
questions.why: The carry threads state between iterations; the per-step outputs are stacked along a new leading axis.

questions.q: When would you use `lax.fori_loop` instead of `scan`?
options: When the loop length is unknown at trace time and depends on data
When you need gradients through a while loop
When you only need the final carry, not per-step outputs
questions.why: `fori_loop` with static bounds lowers to a scan and is differentiable. With dynamic bounds it becomes a `while_loop`, which supports forward-mode but not reverse-mode differentiation.

questions.q: Print statements inside a jitted function run when?
options: Only during tracing, typically once per new shape; use `jax.debug.print` for run-time values
questions.why: Python side effects happen while tracing. `jax.debug.print` is staged into the compiled program.

questions.q: An exponential moving average with bias correction inside `scan` should carry what?
options: The running average and the step count (or the running product of decay factors)
questions.why: The bias-correction factor $1 - \beta^t$ needs $t$. Resetting the average means resetting both parts of the carry.

questions.q: `jax.vmap(f, in_axes=(0, None))(xs, w)` does what?
options: Maps `f` over the leading axis of `xs` while broadcasting the same `w` to every call
Runs `f` once on the whole batch without mapping
questions.why: `None` means the argument isn't batched. This is how you share parameters across examples.

questions.q: Is `jax.vmap` a loop under the hood?
options: No; it rewrites the function into batched operations
It launches one kernel per example
questions.why: vmap transforms each primitive into its batched version (for example matmul into batched matmul), so it runs as one vectorised program.

questions.q: To run an ensemble of 5 models whose parameters are stacked along axis 0, on the same input `x`, use...
options: A Python loop over models only
questions.why: Mapping over the parameter axis and broadcasting the input evaluates every ensemble member at once.

questions.q: Nested `vmap(vmap(dist, (None, 0)), (0, None))(A, B)` computes what for `dist(a, b)`?
options: A matrix of `dist(A[i], B[j])` with shape `(len(A), len(B))`
questions.why: The inner map varies `b` over `B` for a fixed `a`; the outer map varies `a` over `A`.

questions.q: Attention for one sequence is written for `(T, d)` inputs. How do you add batch and head axes?
options: Wrap it in two `vmap`s, one over heads and one over the batch
questions.why: Writing the single-example version and vmapping it keeps the code simple and is as fast as the hand-batched version.

questions.q: What does `out_axes=1` do in `vmap`?
options: Places the mapped axis at position 1 of the output instead of 0
Maps over axis 1 of the input
questions.why: `in_axes` chooses which input axis is mapped; `out_axes` chooses where it appears in the result.

questions.q: Can `vmap` be combined with `grad` and `jit`?
options: No, only one transformation per function
Yes, in any order; they are composable transformations
questions.why: Composability is JAX's central design: `jit(vmap(grad(f)))` is a common pattern.

questions.q: A key-padding mask for batched attention should be passed to the vmapped function how?
options: As another mapped argument with `in_axes=0`, one mask per example
It can't be used with vmap
questions.why: Each example has its own padding, so the mask is batched along with the inputs.

questions.q: What is a pytree in JAX?
options: A nested structure of lists, tuples and dicts (and registered classes) whose leaves are arrays
questions.why: Parameters, gradients and optimiser states are pytrees, and `jax.tree_util.tree_map` applies a function to every leaf.

questions.q: SGD with momentum over a nested parameter dict is written with...
options: `jax.tree_util.tree_map(lambda p, g, v: ..., params, grads, vel)`
questions.why: `tree_map` walks several pytrees of the same structure in lockstep, so the update stays generic for any model.

questions.q: Global-norm clipping needs the norm over **all** leaves. How is it computed?
options: The norm of the first leaf
questions.why: Squares are summed across every leaf before the square root. A non-finite guard then skips the update if the norm is NaN or inf.

questions.q: AdamW with a weight-decay mask usually excludes which parameters from decay?
questions.why: Decaying biases and LayerNorm gains brings little regularisation benefit and can hurt. The mask is a pytree of booleans with the same structure as the parameters.

questions.q: Token-weighted gradient accumulation over micro-batches should divide by...
options: The total number of real tokens across all micro-batches
Each micro-batch's own token count, then average
questions.why: Accumulate the summed per-token gradients and normalise once by the global token count, so every token has equal weight.

questions.q: Why are optimiser states stored as pytrees with the same structure as the parameters?
options: JAX requires it for any array
So updates can be written with `tree_map` and the state can be sharded and checkpointed like the parameters
questions.why: Matching structures make the optimiser generic and let the same sharding rules apply to parameters and their moments.

questions.q: Optax's `optax.chain(optax.clip_by_global_norm(1.0), optax.adamw(1e-3))` applies the transforms in what order?
options: Order depends on the gradient size
Both at once on separate copies
questions.why: Transforms in a chain are applied in sequence to the update, so gradients are clipped before Adam's moments see them.

questions.q: A `NamedTuple` of arrays is a valid pytree. What does `tree_leaves` return for `State(m=a, v=b)`?
questions.why: NamedTuples are registered pytree nodes, so their fields are traversed and the arrays are leaves.

questions.q: Why use dynamic loss scaling for fp16 training?
options: To speed up the forward pass
Small gradients underflow to zero in fp16; scaling the loss up keeps them representable
questions.why: The scale is lowered when an overflow (inf or NaN) appears and raised after a run of stable steps. bf16 has fp32's exponent range and usually doesn't need it.

questions.q: What does `jax.checkpoint` (remat) trade?
options: Memory for compute: activations are recomputed during the backward pass instead of stored
Nothing; it only saves to disk
questions.why: Wrapping each layer of a deep stack (often inside `scan`) cuts activation memory to roughly one layer's worth plus the layer inputs.

questions.q: W8A8 quantised matmul with per-channel weight scales $s_w$ and per-token activation scales $s_a$ dequantises how?
questions.why: The integer accumulation is rescaled by the outer product of the two scale vectors, which works because each scale factors out of its row or column.

questions.q: Why accumulate int8 products in int32?
options: Sums of many int8 products overflow 8 or 16 bits
questions.why: Each product fits in 16 bits, and summing thousands of them needs at least 32 bits.

questions.q: Blockwise attention in `lax.scan` keeps what carry per query row?
options: The running max, the running sum of exponentials and the unnormalised output
questions.why: That is the online softmax, which processes key blocks one at a time with constant memory per row.

questions.q: bf16 has how many mantissa bits, compared with fp16's 10?
questions.why: bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits and cuts the mantissa, trading precision for range; fp16 has a 5-bit exponent and more precision.

questions.q: Summing $10^7$ values of 1.0 in float32 sequentially gives...
options: Exactly $10^7$, but summing $10^8$ ones stalls at $2^{24} = 16{,}777{,}216$
questions.why: Above $2^{24}$, adding 1 to a float32 is lost to rounding. Reductions use pairwise summation or higher-precision accumulators.

questions.q: A matmul in fp32 on TPU may use bf16 passes by default. Which setting forces full precision?
questions.why: TPUs default to faster reduced-precision passes for fp32 matmuls; the precision argument trades speed for accuracy.

questions.q: RoPE rotates each pair of dimensions by angle $p\theta_i$. Why can JAX compute it for arbitrary positions without a cache?
options: The angles are a cheap function of the position array, so they're computed on the fly
It needs a lookup table in JAX
questions.why: `cos` and `sin` of `positions[:, None] * freqs[None, :]` are cheap and fuse into the surrounding kernels under jit.

questions.q: Writing a new key into a batched KV cache at per-sequence positions uses...
options: `cache.at[pos].set(k_new)` with a scalar `pos` for all sequences
questions.why: Advanced indexing with a batch index and a position per sequence scatters each new key into its own slot; concatenation would change the shape every step.

questions.q: Top-p (nucleus) sampling with $p = 0.9$ keeps which tokens?
options: The smallest set of most-likely tokens whose probabilities sum to at least 0.9
The top 90% of the vocabulary by count
questions.why: Sort by probability, take the cumulative sum and keep tokens up to where it first reaches $p$; then renormalise.

questions.q: Applying temperature $T$ divides the logits by $T$. What does $T \to 0$ approach?
questions.why: Small temperatures sharpen the softmax until all mass sits on the largest logit.

questions.q: In a decode step, grouped-query attention with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads reads how much KV cache compared with full multi-head attention?
questions.why: Only 8 key and value heads are stored and read, and each serves 4 query heads.

questions.q: Why does every decode step need a fixed-size KV cache buffer in JAX rather than growing it?
options: Growing arrays change shapes, which would trigger recompilation every step
KV caches must be powers of two
questions.why: Preallocating the maximum length and tracking positions keeps shapes static for jit.

questions.q: A causal mask for a decode step with cache length $L$ and current position $p$ allows attention to which positions?
questions.why: Slots after the current position are empty (or stale) and must be masked out.

questions.q: Sampling with a JAX key in a decode loop: what should happen to the key each step?
options: Reuse the same key every step
Create a new key from the step number with `PRNGKey(step)`, ignoring the original seed
Split it, using one subkey for this step's sample and carrying the other forward
questions.why: Reusing a key repeats the same random draws. Splitting in the loop carry gives fresh, reproducible randomness.

questions.q: Batched greedy decoding in `lax.scan` must handle sequences that hit EOS at different steps. How?
options: Remove finished sequences from the batch
Carry a `done` mask and replace tokens of finished sequences with padding
Stop the scan early for each sequence
Run each sequence in its own scan
questions.why: Shapes must stay fixed, so finished rows keep running but their outputs are masked.

questions.q: Why can't `lax.scan` stop early when all sequences finish?
options: Its length is fixed at trace time; use `lax.while_loop` for a data-dependent stop
questions.why: `while_loop` supports dynamic termination but not reverse-mode autodiff, which decoding doesn't need.

questions.q: Decode attention over a paged KV cache gathers keys how?
options: From one contiguous array per sequence
Through a block table that maps each sequence's logical blocks to physical blocks
questions.why: The block table adds one level of indirection, which lets sequences share a memory pool without contiguous reservations.

questions.q: In one beam-search step with beam width $k$ and vocabulary $V$, how many candidate continuations are scored?
questions.why: Each beam is extended by every token, then the best $k$ of the $kV$ candidates are kept.

questions.q: How should finished beams be treated in a vectorised beam-search step?
options: Keep them with their score frozen and allow only a padding continuation
questions.why: Fixed shapes require keeping them. Allowing only one zero-cost continuation preserves their score while unfinished beams compete.

questions.q: In speculative decoding, a draft token with draft probability $q$ and target probability $p$ is accepted with probability...
questions.why: On rejection, sampling from the normalised $\max(0, p - q)$ makes the output exactly target-distributed.

questions.q: Why is the whole decode loop usually jitted as one function?
options: It makes the model more accurate
It avoids Python overhead and host-device round trips between steps
questions.why: A per-step Python loop pays dispatch overhead every token; compiling the loop keeps everything on the device.

questions.q: How is the KV cache usually threaded through `lax.scan` in a decode loop?
options: As part of the carry, updated each step with `.at[].set`
questions.why: The carry holds state that changes across iterations: the cache, the current token, positions and `done` flags.

questions.q: With a mesh of axes `('data', 'model')` and `PartitionSpec('data', None)` on a `(B, D)` array, how is it laid out?
options: Rows split across the `data` axis; columns replicated
questions.why: Each entry of the spec names the mesh axis that shards that array dimension; `None` means replicated along it.

questions.q: In data-parallel SGD with `shard_map` or `pmap`, which collective averages gradients across devices?
options: None; each device keeps its own gradient
questions.why: Every replica must apply the same update, so gradients are reduced across the data axis before the optimiser step.

questions.q: A Megatron-style tensor-parallel MLP splits the first weight by columns and the second by rows. Where is the communication?
options: One all-reduce after the second matmul
An all-gather before the first matmul only
questions.why: Column-splitting the first layer gives each device a slice of the hidden units with no communication; row-splitting the second produces partial sums that one all-reduce combines.

questions.q: A ring all-reduce built from `ppermute` sends data how?
options: Each device broadcasts to all others at once
Each device passes chunks to its neighbour around a ring, in a reduce-scatter then an all-gather phase
Only one device participates per step
Every device sends everything to device 0
questions.why: The ring keeps every link busy and moves about $2(N - 1)/N$ times the data size per device, independent of $N$.

questions.q: What does `jax.lax.all_gather` do?
options: Sends shards to the next device
Collects each device's shard so every device gets the full array
questions.why: All-gather is the inverse of sharding, as needed when a replicated value is required, for example before a matmul with a sharded input.

questions.q: Under `jit` with sharded inputs, who decides where collectives go?
options: The XLA compiler (GSPMD), from the input and output shardings
You must insert every collective manually
questions.why: With `jit` and sharding annotations, XLA propagates shardings and inserts communication. `shard_map` is the manual alternative.

questions.q: Fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP or ZeRO-3) shards what?
options: Parameters, gradients and optimiser state across the data-parallel devices
questions.why: Each device stores a slice of everything and all-gathers parameters just before they are needed.

questions.q: Increasing data-parallel devices from 8 to 16 at a fixed per-device batch does what to the global batch?
questions.why: The global batch is per-device batch times the number of replicas, which may require retuning the learning rate.
